questions.question: Why does the testing pyramid have MANY unit tests at the bottom and FEW end-to-end tests at the top?
options: Unit tests are more important than E2E tests
Unit tests are fast and cheap, catching most bugs efficiently; E2E tests are slow and expensive, reserved for what only shows up in the full real system
E2E tests don't actually test anything useful
It's an arbitrary convention with no real reasoning
questions.explanation: The shape reflects a cost/speed tradeoff: fast, cheap unit tests should catch the bulk of bugs; fewer, slower integration and E2E tests fill in what unit tests structurally can't catch (wiring, routing, real system interaction).

questions.question: Which of these is an INTEGRATION test, not a unit test?
options: Testing a Library class with a fake ILateFeePolicy injected
Using WebApplicationFactory to send a real HTTP request through your app's actual routing, model binding, and database
Testing a single method's return value with no dependencies at all
Testing that a record's Equals works correctly
questions.explanation: WebApplicationFactory tests exercise multiple REAL pieces together (routing, DI, database) rather than one class in isolation with fakes — that's the defining trait of an integration test.

questions.question: What does a contract test verify that a normal integration test testing `student.Name == "Ali"` does NOT?
options: That the response's SHAPE (required fields, JSON types) is correct — independent of which specific student or data values come back
That the server is running on the correct port
questions.explanation: A contract test focuses on structure — field presence and types — rather than specific values. It catches breaking API shape changes (a renamed or retyped field) that a value-specific assertion wouldn't necessarily be designed to catch.

questions.question: Why use `JsonDocument.Parse(...)` instead of `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(...)` for a contract test?
options: Contract tests check STRUCTURE without assuming a specific target type already matches — JsonDocument gives a low-level, navigable view of any JSON, which is exactly what's needed to verify shape rather than deserialize into an assumed-correct type
questions.explanation: Deserialize<T> presupposes T already correctly describes the shape — if the actual response doesn't match T, you might get silent default values rather than a clear failure. JsonDocument lets you explicitly check field-by-field what's actually present.

questions.question: A breaking change to an API's response shape (e.g., renaming a field) can pass all of an app's internal logic-focused tests while still breaking every external consumer of that API.
questions.explanation: Internal logic tests check behavior/values, not necessarily the exact response shape. This is exactly the gap contract tests are designed to close — verifying the shape consumers depend on hasn't silently changed.
